problem: LLMs hold useful semantic priors about where objects tend to be (a stove is in the kitchen, near the fridge), but they know nothing about the layout of the specific scene. Prior methods that let the LLM greedily choose where to go (LGX-style) fail when it guesses wrong. Methods that score with a small LM's token likelihoods (L3MVN with GPT-2 logprobs) extract little of that semantic knowledge.
motivation: Classical frontier-based exploration in unfamiliar environments is uninformed and slow. Humans navigate new buildings quickly by reasoning about semantics. The observation driving the paper is that an LLM's ungrounded 'narratives' are unreliable as plans but useful as suggestions. They should therefore enter a planner as a soft heuristic that helps when correct and can be overridden by geometric search when wrong.
key_idea: Language Frontier Guide (LFG) samples an LLM repeatedly with chain-of-thought positive ('where to search') and negative ('where not to search') prompts over object clusters near each frontier, and adds the resulting empirical likelihoods as a heuristic term, alongside distance, in frontier-based exploration.
insight: Treating the LLM as a heuristic rather than a planner is what matters. In Table 1, Greedy LLM, which follows the LLM directly, gets 54.4 SR, below plain FBE at 61.1. LFG's heuristic reaches 68.9, and FBE takes over when the LLM is wrong (Fig. 6). The Table 2 ablations show how the score is extracted also matters: logprob scoring (60.4) and random scoring (61.1, equal to FBE) give nothing over uninformed search, dropping CoT costs 6.6 points, positive-only prompts cost 4.7, and directly asking for scores ('Ask', 62.4) costs 6.5. Polled, CoT-justified, positive-minus-negative votes are needed to turn LLM guesswork into a useful signal.
method: Episodic memory: either a 2D metric occupancy + semantic grid (sim, following SemExp/Gervet et al.) or a topological graph of omnidirectional views with Detic object labels (real, following ViKiNG).

Subgoal grounding: frontier points are tied to nearby object clusters. In sim, class centers are agglomeratively clustered with a 6 m threshold; in real, the objects seen by each of the 4 cameras form one cluster. Clusters are rendered as text lists such as 'sofa, tv, speaker'.

LLM polling: gpt-3.5-turbo is sampled ns=10 times with a structured one-shot prompt that requires 'Reasoning: … Answer: i'. Vote frequencies give empirical likelihoods instead of logprobs, which the API does not expose and which are incompatible with CoT.

Positive + negative prompts with chain-of-thought: separate prompts ask which clusters are most likely and which are least likely to lead to the goal. The negative votes down-weight clearly irrelevant regions when the LLM is uncertain among positives.

Heuristic frontier scoring: h(f_i,q) = wp·LLMpos(c_i) − wn·LLMneg(c_i) − dist(f_i,p), with wp=300 and wn=150. The language term applies only if the nearest cluster lies within δ=2 m of the frontier; otherwise the score is plain FBE (−distance). The system replans every step (τ=1) and goes directly to the goal once it is detected.
Low-level control: a deterministic local planner in sim; in the real world, the NoMaD goal-masked diffusion policy (Transformer-based, ViNT-style) reaches the chosen frontier view.

setting.backbone: gpt-3.5-turbo (frozen, via API) as heuristic scorer inside a frontier-based exploration planner. Real world adds a Detic open-vocabulary detector (pretrained) and the NoMaD diffusion low-level policy (pretrained).
setting.training_data: none (training-free); HM3D training scenes are not used
setting.observation: Sim: egocentric RGB-D + accurate pose + ground-truth semantic labels. Real: 4 RGB webcams at 90° spacing (omnidirectional) with Detic labels.
setting.action_space: Sim: frontier subgoals on a 2D metric map, reached by a deterministic local controller (Habitat discrete actions, max 500 steps). Real: choice among topological frontier views (forward/left/right/turn around), executed by the NoMaD policy.
setting.privileged: In simulation, ground-truth semantic segmentation and accurate pose ('we use ground-truth semantic information for all simulated baselines'). None in the real world.

numbers_note: Table 2 ablations report Success only, not SPL. The remaining ablations (Random 61.1, Ask 62.4) are omitted here. The real-world experiments (cafeteria/office, apartment) have no numeric table; the text says only that 'LFG achieves 16% better performance' than the greedy LLM baseline and that FBE times out (30-min limit). The HM3D protocol runs 10 episodes per scene; the split is not named, and the paper says there are '10 categories'. In Table 1, SemExp's SPL is printed as 0.29 and L3MVN's SPL is blank.
results: On HM3D ObjectNav, training-free LFG (gpt-3.5-turbo) reaches 68.9 SR / 36.0 SPL. This beats OVRL-v2 (64.7/28.1, 12M frames), SemExp (63.1), L3MVN (62.4), FBE (61.1/34.0), Greedy LLM/LGX (54.4/26.9) and DD-PPO (27.9). Ablations show polling (+7.8 over random), CoT (+6.6) and negative prompts (+4.7) are each important; logprob scoring (60.4) does not beat plain FBE. In real-world tests on a LoCoBot, FBE times out and LFG is about 16% better than greedy LLM exploration.
limitations: Simulated results use ground-truth semantic segmentation and a small evaluation (10 episodes per scene), so the gains are measured under perfect perception.
Only indoor environments are tested; how useful LLM semantic priors are in other domains (e.g., forests) is unknown.

Repeated cloud LLM calls with CoT (10 samples × 2 prompts per replanning step, about 30M tokens per eval) are slow and need internet access. Real-world goals are restricted to a whitelisted subset of Detic classes, and real-world results are not reported quantitatively.
